commits.subject: site v0.5.13: the guest in the tab is on the page's network; the interceptor shows and vetoes every packet
commits.body:
Merges dev (v0.5.10 to v0.5.12 from the other agents: sharness.dev's article, the agents register,
the outreach plan, the telemetry lane) with this session's v0.5.10, renumbered.

The demo and the playground give the guest a virtio-net card whose packets become the browser's
fetch(): the page is router, DHCP, DNS and the TLS client for every HTTP request on port 80.
The playground's interceptor (netwatch.js) decodes every frame into a table with a detail pane
and enforces an egress allowlist outside the guest. Three verdicts in one session: allowed by
the page, blocked by the page (403), refused by the kernel before any packet left the process,
with the DNS query Landlock does not see still visible. P5, a web-fetch profile. 17 checks held
against this tree. Evidence §9, the playground page, Linux in the browser, the status page, the
adoption review and the article (an update with the panel's screenshot) record it.

commits.subject: site v0.5.10: one standard, many languages; sharness.dev joins as an author; R8 asks for the languages decision
commits.body:
A new author, sharness.dev, the developer agent, with the brief to build reference
implementations of SHarness in several languages. Its first article, One standard, many
languages, separates what in each component is a specification (the policy's shape and hash,
the manifest and the edges, the KMS, net, fs, llm and bash protocols, hello's six expectations)
from what is an implementation (reaching the kernel, serving mutual TLS, holding a secret),
maps every component against Python, JavaScript in Node and in the browser, Rust and Go, says
what each runtime adds to the attack surface, draws the adoption ladder from a policy file to a
component, and proposes standards versioned with test vectors and a reviewed registry. Two
figures. Languages carries the proposed set and order; roadmap decision 11 is extended, still
open; comms R8 asks Dinis for the decision. The seven example policies' hashes are quoted as
the first test vectors (CLI dev at ebd1445, Python 3.13, 25 Oct 2026). Nothing is built in any
language beyond the Python experiments and the browser's hash.

may do: ABP from riskmandate.ai applied to processes; SHarness is one enforcer built to be read,
the reference implementation; any environment that enforces the same rows is valid, so enforcers
mix and match under one hash; every product is an integration point or a translation target),
the three questions to ask of any policy and environment (express, enforce as what barrier kind,
verify), the enforceability matrix (policy rows against SHarness, bubblewrap, Docker, Claude
Code's sandbox, Kubernetes, microVMs, ToolHive, OpenShell, with the barrier kind per cell), the
integration points product by product, and the market analysis moved here from evidence/.

/code/browser/: a real Linux kernel runs in a tab today; Landlock has no architecture dependency
(security/landlock/Kconfig depends only on SECURITY; the syscalls are in the i386 table), and
Alpine's 32-bit linux-virt ships with it on, so sharness-ai hello in a browser (v86) is a build:
the options compared, the recommended build, what a browser can never show (E09, researched).

E10 in the CLI, policy translate: the same policy as bwrap, docker, claude-code or kubernetes,
with the list of what that target does not enforce; on the experiments, code and status pages.

commits.subject: site v0.5.1: the brief, the whole surface of a process, the spectrum, and the versioning rule
commits.body:
/brief/: SHarness in one read, for Dinis, with four drawn diagrams (SVG, not ASCII): the
moving parts and how they work together, one request end to end (sgit clone --sealed through
app, net, kms, server and fs, with the KMS frozen and thawed), the whole surface of a process,
and the spectrum from a hello world to sgit; then where it is now and what to decide.

/surface/: what a process can do, one row per interface (files, network, processes, signals
and IPC, memory, time, devices, identity, kernel services, environment, the model, secrets):
what bounds it in SHarness, whether that was measured, and what the bound does not cover.
What is left when everything else is limited is the process's policy: a virtual operating
system for one process.

/spectrum/: five profiles of one harness (a hello world, a Claude Code session, a tool, a
newsroom agent, sgit), what each runs, its threat, policy, components, mode and status; and
the compatibility map for sgit's next version (steps 0 to 5, each leaving sgit as 0.24.0 when
nothing is switched on). Measured 24 Oct 2026: sgit 0.24.0's --version and pki list run
unchanged under a v0 deny-all policy.

Versioning rule (Dinis Cruz, 24 Oct 2026): every push to dev is a patch release (vX.Y.Z+1);
a merge to main is a minor release (vX.Y+1.0), tagged on main. Enforced in the tag job,
documented in the README, the admin page and the release history.

commits.subject: site v0.5.0: market and competitive analysis
commits.body:
/market/: what exists that does part of what SHarness is designed to do, as of 24 Oct 2026:
agent and code sandboxes and runtimes (Claude Code's sandbox-runtime, Codex, Gemini CLI,
Antigravity, Cursor, E2B, Modal, Daytona, Fly Sprites, Vercel, Cloudflare, Docker Sandboxes,
microsandbox, OpenSandbox, Kubernetes Agent Sandbox, Azure and Foundry, NVIDIA OpenShell,
the primitives); policy and guardrails; MCP and tool security; LLM gateways and key holders;
secrets, workload identity, confidential computing and agent identity; enterprise platforms
(enforcement versus monitoring); standards and reports. Every row carries its source and the
date read; secondary figures are marked; five load-bearing rows were re-checked on their
primary pages and the text corrected where the first pass overstated (NemoClaw's page does
not name Landlock or seccomp; the DeepSeek CVE page could not be read).

Then: where SHarness sits (five distinctive claims, all designed), what to reuse rather than
rebuild, direct competitors and complements, honest gaps, market signals with numbers
(acquisitions, rounds, standards, platform moves, incidents), and seven threats to the thesis.

Registered in the nav, footer, llms.txt, sitemap, the front page and the release history;
R6 on the comms board now covers it.

commits.body:

the findings and what this release did about each are on /research/. The largest finding is
an omission: Claude Code's own sandbox (bubblewrap, a network namespace, a hostname-allowlist
proxy) as prior art and plug-in point; the comparison is on /experiments/, with rows on
Agents §2 and Policies §9. Agents §2 row 3 (a PreToolUse hook rewriting Bash) is now
documented rather than "verify": updatedInput replaces the whole input.

Experiments: /experiments/ lays out the ladder (browser mockups, any Claude session, Linux,
planned, the launcher above the agent) and experiments E01 to E08; E01 to E04 are runnable in
the CLI (probe, policy hash, run, hello) and E04 is measured on Evidence §9 (5 of 5 held in
one cloud session, 24 Oct 2026, with the caveat that a policy a process applies to its own
children is a Setting for itself).

Mockups: /mockups/policy-hash.html (canonical JSON + SHA-256 in WebCrypto; the same hash as
sharness-ai policy hash, checked headless) and /mockups/edges.html (the edge matrix and the
layer that refuses each edge).

commits.subject: The guest on a network the page provides, and an interceptor that sees and vetoes every packet
commits.body:
The guest gets a virtio-net card (the driver and its two dependencies unpacked from Alpine's
kernel package into the initramfs; init brings eth0 up on v86's fake subnet) and v86's fetch
backend behind it: the page answers as router, DHCP and DNS, and turns each HTTP request on port
80 into the browser's own fetch(), upgraded to TLS so the page is the TLS client where the name
is seen. Other ports are reset. The scripted run and boot_node.mjs (NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 behind
a proxy) fetch sharness.ai/llms.txt with no policy, are refused by the kernel under P1 (443
only) and succeed under P5, a new profile for a tool that fetches pages (80 and 443).

netwatch.js: every frame the guest sends or receives is decoded (ARP, DHCP, DNS with record
types, ICMP, TCP flags, HTTP request and status lines) into a flows table with a detail pane,
and the backend's fetch is wrapped with an egress allowlist of hostnames, enforced outside the
guest: a host off the list gets a 403 before any fetch(). The playground shows all three verdicts
in one session: allowed by the page, blocked by the page, and refused by the kernel before any
packet left the process (with the DNS query still visible, since Landlock does not see UDP).
test_playground.mjs checks each: 17 of 17 in headless Chromium.

commits.subject: Fix three bugs the new CI found: Python 3.11 support, hello in a virtualenv, the test environment
commits.body:
The first runs of tests.yml failed, and each failure was real:

- hello.py used a multi-line string inside an f-string replacement field, which only Python
  3.12 parses (PEP 701); on 3.11, the version the package claims, importing hello failed.
- policy translate FILE --to T -- CMD: argparse before 3.12 rejects `-- CMD` after an option,
  so the wrapped command is now split off before parsing.
- hello_policy granted sys.base_prefix but not sys.prefix, so from a virtualenv outside the
  system paths Python could not read pyvenv.cfg and every probe died before running.
- The workflow installed only pytest, so `python -m sharness_ai hello` from a temporary
  directory could not import the package. The workflow now installs the package, and also runs
  the suite uninstalled; the test puts the checkout on PYTHONPATH and prints stderr on failure.
  fail-fast is off so one Python's failure no longer hides another's.

60 tests pass on Python 3.11 and 3.12 (clean virtualenvs, package not installed) and 3.13.

commits.subject: Add the playground: sharness-ai in Pyodide and in a shell on the Linux guest; tests on dev
commits.body:
experiments/browser/playground.{html,js}: two terminals in one page. Pyodide (Python in
WebAssembly) installs a dev wheel of this package with micropip and runs policy hash, check,
translate and probe; the Linux guest boots with sharness.mode=shell and gives a shell on its
serial line where run and hello are enforced by the guest kernel. A policy panel hashes the
same JSON with WebCrypto, in Pyodide and in the guest, and copies an edited policy into both.
test_playground.mjs drives both tabs in headless Chromium: 11 of 11 checks.

build_wheel.py builds the wheel with the standard library as <version>+dev.<commit>, with a
wheel.json manifest; build_guest.py assembles it, the playground and the policies into www/.

run and hello now refuse cleanly where there is no kernel and no processes (Pyodide,
emscripten), exit 126, instead of a traceback; limits imports resource only where it exists;
probe prints unknown rather than None and says when there is no kernel or no Landlock.

.github/workflows/tests.yml runs the unit tests on every push to dev and every pull request,
on Python 3.11 to 3.13; until now they ran only on a release to main. Package metadata points
at the site's current paths. 59 tests pass.

commits.subject: Add E09, the harness under a second kernel, and the example policies P0 to P4
commits.body:
experiments/browser/: one Alpine 3.23 x86 guest (Alpine's linux-virt 6.18 with Landlock,
Python 3.12, this package, the example policies) built by build_guest.py (standard library:
fetches the pinned packages, unpacks them with tarfile, writes the initramfs with its own cpio
writer) and run three ways: v86 in Node (boot_node.mjs), v86 in a browser tab (page.html,
boot_browser.mjs through Playwright), and the same i386 binaries through chroot on the host
kernel (chroot_native.sh). v86 is pinned in its own package.json and lives only here.

Measured 25 Oct 2026 in one cloud session: landlock up, probe ABI 7 and cgroups v2 in the
guest; hello 6 of 6 in Node (58 s), in headless Chromium (76 s) and in the chroot; run under
P1 allowed 443 and refused 80, under P2 refused writes; the seven policies hash the same as
on the host. Found: the ELF interpreter (/lib/ld-musl-*) must be executable, and v86 needs
no COOP/COEP headers.

experiments/policies/: five profiles in the v0 shape with /work as the workspace: P0 a hello
world with caps, P1 a coding agent's session, P2 a tool or MCP server on stdio, P3 the sgit.ai
newsroom agent, P4 the sgit CLI; a README on how they compose and what v0 cannot say yet. Run
natively: every expectation held; sgit 0.24.0 ran under P4.

Tests: the examples (shape, pinned hashes, executable interpreter, no writable-and-executable
path) and the guest build (cpio round trip, determinism, the pieces). 53 pass.

commits.subject: Add policy translate (E10): the same policy as bwrap, docker, claude-code or kubernetes, with the gap
commits.body:
The policy is the centre and every enforcer is a target. `sharness-ai policy translate FILE
--to bwrap|docker|claude-code|kubernetes|landlock [-- CMD...]` writes the v0 policy in that
target's native form (a bubblewrap or docker run command line, a Claude Code sandbox
settings.json fragment, a Kubernetes Pod securityContext plus NetworkPolicy) and then lists
what that target does not enforce from the policy: the enforceability matrix on
sharness.ai/landscape/enforceability, row by row, made executable. Nothing is run against the
target. translate.py, 176 lines; 6 tests (40 in all). E09 (a real kernel in a browser tab)
and E10 added to experiments/README.md.

commits.subject: Add memory and process-count caps to run and hello (E03, E04), and point docs at the new site paths
commits.body:
process.max_memory_mb and process.max_pids in a v0 policy: RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_NPROC on the
child, plus a memory and a pids cgroup (v1 or v2) under /sys/fs/cgroup/<controller>/sharness-ai/<pid>
where /sys/fs/cgroup is writable, removed by the parent afterwards (limits.py, 95 lines). hello
now runs with a 128 MiB cap and a sixth probe: a 400 MiB allocation must be refused. Measured
25 Oct 2026 in one Claude Code cloud session: MemoryError under the cap, "Cannot fork" for the
fifth process under max_pids: 4, no cgroup left behind; 6 of 6 held. 34 tests.

commits.subject: Add the first experiments: probe, policy hash, run and hello, with tests and a skill
commits.body:
Experiments E01 to E04 from the design (sharness.ai/experiments), standard library only:
  probe             E01  the grant: uid, capabilities, NoNewPrivs, seccomp, Landlock ABI,
                         memfd_secret, namespaces, cgroups, tools, proxy variable names
  policy hash|check E02  a v0 Process Behaviour Policy canonicalised and hashed (sha256:…);
                         the browser mockup on sharness.ai produces the same hash
  run               E03  one command under a policy: Landlock read/write/exec per path and
                         TCP connect per port through ctypes, no_new_privs, an empty network
                         namespace for network "none" where one can be made; --expect-hash
                         refuses to run anything unless the file hashes to it
  hello             E04  the memo's acceptance test for one child process: read allowed,
                         writes refused, connect refused, wrong hash runs nothing; prints the
                         caveat (a Boundary for the child, a Setting for whoever ran it)

Also: experiments/README.md (the numbered ladder, E05 to E08 planned, what was measured),
two example policies, the sharness-hello skill for Claude Code sessions, CLAUDE.md, the
README and the package description at the experiments stage. 29 tests; those that need
Landlock skip where it is absent. Status: experiments; no SHarness component is built.
